title: GCD (Recursion)
directAnswer: Base case `b == 0` returns `a`; else return `gcd(b, a % b)`. Euclid's algorithm — O(log min(a,b)).

remember.takeaway: Euclid: replace the pair with (b, a mod b) until b is 0.

problemStatement: Given two non-negative integers `a` and `b`, compute their greatest common divisor recursively (Euclid's algorithm).
understanding: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), bottoming out when b == 0 (then a is the answer).

approaches.name: Euclid's algorithm
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Euclid's algorithm expressed recursively: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), with base case gcd(a, 0) = a.

**Why mod-reduction preserves the GCD.** Any common divisor of a and b also divides a mod b (= a − ⌊a/b⌋·b), and vice versa, so the pair (a, b) and (b, a mod b) share the same set of common divisors — hence the same greatest one. Each step shrinks the numbers fast.

**Why the base case is b == 0.** Every integer divides 0, so gcd(a, 0) = a. When the remainder reaches 0, the previous divisor is the answer, which the recursion returns automatically.

**Why O(log) depth.** The remainder at least halves every two steps, so the recursion bottoms out in logarithmic depth — far fewer calls than testing divisors. LCM follows immediately: lcm(a,b) = a/gcd·b.
hints: Express gcd(a,b) using b and the remainder a mod b.
What pair makes the recursion stop?
Why does replacing a with a mod b keep the GCD the same?
approaches.insight: LCM follows immediately: lcm(a,b) = a / gcd(a,b) * b.
approaches.complexityReasoning: the remainder shrinks geometrically, so O(log min(a,b)) recursive calls.

java.explanation: When the remainder hits 0, a is the GCD.

pitfalls: Swapping the arguments wrongly (gcd(a % b, b) loops).
Dividing by zero by mishandling b == 0.
